chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
title: Four years at the Grunewald and seven years at Cobb's Tea Room
summary: He explains how he persuaded Mr. Cobb to open the tea room, drew his own following and effectively ran the place without a contract.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Four years in Grunewald and seven years at Cobb's, Cobb's Tea Room. Eleven to one at night. We didn't get six sets in. We'd get a beer and get three sets and the night's over. And then when we had competitions with the other places trying to put us out of business, they brought in acts. And Mr. Cobb knew as much about running a nightclub as I knew about flying an airplane. He'd have a bill of fare that... I said, Mr. Cobb, we need a bill of fare that big with sandwiches. Find out what they're drinking. All the college kids brought orange aid for ninety cents and sat there all night with it. Friday night we had to take the tablecloths off the table. They'd take everything out of the place. But we had the young people and that's what people like. People like young people. Old people like young people. I like the old people because they spend their money. But I worked the first two weeks in Cobb. They cut out the music in the Grunewald and Mr. Cobb had been after me. So I went home and I said, Mr. Cobb, we're through. He said, why? I said, we're just through. I said, now's your chance to get a hold of us. Why not open the tea room? Because he had tried it with several orchestras and they didn't draw their breath. He said, the place is not in condition and we were in Lent. 19th of March. I said, Mr. Cobb, I'll bring you enough masons and Jews to pack the place. Don't worry about the Catholics with the Lent. He said, what do you mean? I said, I have the clientele. I have the follower. And I did. I don't mind telling you. I'd stand in front of the cats and best off on Canal Street and see anybody come and say,

Where you been? Well, he said, it's only so he made a table. It got so we didn't have enough tables and the head waiter started making all the money. Because my friends would say, you asked me to come. He tells me I don't have a table. And I had made the reservations for them. So I told Mr. Cobb, I want to know who he'd wear them. I practically ran that joint because he knew nothing about it. All he did was sit there and smoke, chain smoking cigars, you know. Fine man, finest. Could have lost a short, I waited for seven years without a contract, which was to my advantage. Because every time I got an offer from New York, Chicago or Birmingham, better than his, I'd show it to him. I can't beat that. I'd say, what can you do?
